analysis.one_liner: Limits how companies and governments collect, use, and sell Americans' COVID-19 health and location data.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2020 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 pandemic, apps and websites were collecting people's test results, symptoms, location, and contacts. This bill would have required companies handling that 'emergency health data' to get people's clear consent, keep it secure, and delete it shortly after the emergency ends. It would have banned using that data for advertising or to deny people jobs, housing, credit, insurance, or the right to vote, and let people sue violators in court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose health, location, or contact data was gathered through COVID-19 screening, testing, or contact-tracing tools — essentially the whole public. The bill gave people the right to know what was collected, correct errors, revoke consent, and sue for violations of $100–$5,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose health and location data was collected

how_it_helps.text: Required organizations collecting COVID-related health data — including test results, symptoms, precise location, and contact lists — to get a person's clear, affirmative consent before collecting it, and to let people revoke that consent [S3].
Banned using emergency health data for commercial advertising, e-commerce targeting, or to deny people employment, credit, insurance, housing, or access to public accommodations [S3].
Prohibited government entities and covered organizations from denying or interfering with the right to vote based on someone's health data or participation in contact tracing [S3].
Required destruction of the data within 60 days after the emergency ends (or after collection), and required large data holders to publicly report every 90 days what they collected and shared [S3].

Gave the Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individuals the power to enforce the rules, and made pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for these claims, preserving people's right to sue in court [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, companies running contact-tracing apps, health-screening tools, and ad-tech pipelines that profit from health and location data would bear the compliance and liability costs; they could no longer monetize the data or force disputes into arbitration.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tech platforms, data brokers, ad-tech firms

drawbacks.text: The bill layered new compliance duties on contact-tracing and screening tools during an active pandemic; developers of those tools argued-style concerns about costs and rapid FTC rulemaking (the bill required a full rulemaking completed within 45 days of enactment) could slow deployment of public-health technology [S3].
Penalties of up to $5,000 per violation and a broad private right of action exposed companies to class litigation over technical compliance failures, a cost honest supporters would acknowledge [S3].

The bill did not cover health care providers, HIPAA-covered entities, or public health authorities, leaving manual contact tracing and HIPAA-regulated handling under separate rules; critics of such carve-outs note the resulting patchwork can confuse people about whose privacy rules apply [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — keeping COVID-era health, location, and contact data out of advertising systems and away from landlords, employers, insurers, and voter-targeting — was substantial at a moment when such data was being collected at unprecedented scale. The compliance burden on contact-tracing developers and the aggressive 45-day FTC rulemaking deadline were real design costs, and the exclusions created a patchwork, but the core protections were well-targeted at genuinely sensitive data.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2020, referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on May 14, 2020, with Senator Mark Warner, during the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic when contact-tracing apps and health screening tools were collecting large amounts of health and location data [S1][S3].
Twelve senators cosponsored the bill: eleven Democrats and one Independent; no Republicans cosponsored [S4].
The bill's only action beyond introduction was being read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on May 14, 2020 [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that collect, monetize, or share COVID-related health and location data — contact-tracing app operators, ad-tech firms, and data brokers — are better off because the bill died, since they face no federal privacy rules for this data and keep forced-arbitration clauses. The only actor who acted on the bill was the committee, by never taking it up; no recorded opposition or lobbying campaign appears in the provided record, so who pressed for its burial cannot be documented from these sources.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and ad-tech firms handling health data

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Public Health Emergency Privacy Act on May 14, 2020

for.name: Sen. Mark Warner
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-lead cosponsor at introduction

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 14, 2020 and never scheduled a hearing or committee vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all thirteen supporters were Democrats or the Independent who caucuses with Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored [S4].

industries.industry: Tech platforms and contact-tracing app developers
industries.note: The bill regulated how these companies handle health and location data, requiring consent, security, and deletion — but it also routed COVID data collection through them and exempted service providers and health care providers. Companies operating contact-tracing apps would gain public trust while bearing compliance costs.

The bill flatly banned using emergency health data for advertising and e-commerce targeting, cutting off a growing market for health-adjacent location and contact data. Consumers' privacy gain is directly this industry's lost revenue.

industries.industry: Employers, landlords, insurers, and consumer credit companies
industries.note: The bill prohibited making jobs, housing, insurance, credit, and education opportunities unavailable based on emergency health data. These firms lost a potential tool for screening people by health status.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and defendants' litigation strategies
industries.note: The bill voided pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for claims under the act, so companies could not channel privacy violations into individual arbitration. This preserved court access for ordinary people.
